Rose approached the bird gently, murmuring soothing words as soft as a lullaby. The little creature’s eyes, wide with fear, glinted like drops of dew. "Don’t worry," Rose whispered, "I'll help you." Carefully, she used her teeth to nibble away at the strands, freeing the bird. It shook its feathers gratefully and chirped a melody that seemed to thank her. As it flew into the cerulean sky, a warm breeze enveloped Rose, as if the kingdom itself was smiling upon her. The rainbow bridge swirled with deeper hues of gold and green, glistening with renewed brilliance. Rose continued, heart swelling with newfound courage and joy.

Now on the other side of the bridge, Rose entered a land unlike any she had seen before. The trees were draped with colorful ribbons, and flowers in every shade of the rainbow swayed gently in the breeze, nodding their blooms in greeting. The kingdom's inhabitants — from giggling foxes in dapper hats to gracious deer with gentle eyes — all paused to wave and welcome her. Rose felt as though she had walked into the pages of a wonderfully vibrant storybook. The air buzzed with a joyful harmony, and her paws tingled with excitement as she followed the winding path into the heart of the kingdom.

Deep in the kingdom, beside a stream that babbled stories of ancient days, Rose found a wise old turtle named Elder Willow resting beside a towering sunflower. Elder Willow wore a crown of clover and radiated kindness like a warm summer day. With a gentle nod, he invited Rose to sit with him. "Welcome, young Rose," he rumbled, his voice a comforting lullaby. "Here in Kindness Kingdom, we believe that kindness is the sunshine in which love grows." Rose listened intently as Willow shared tales of how acts of kindness could change not only hearts but entire lives. She learned that kindness came in many forms, from a simple smile to a helping hand, each gesture as precious as the next.

Eager to carry the spirit of kindness within her, Rose trekked further into the kingdom, where she stumbled upon a bustling marketplace. Tables piled high with delectable treats and handmade crafts stretched as far as the eye could see. Sweet scents filled the air — honey cakes, berry pies, and nut clusters. The merchants, buoyant with cheer, offered her samples, each accompanied by a story of its making. A thoughtful gift caught her eye: a small clay pot painted with dainty daisies. Remembering how much her grandmother loved tending plants, Rose exchanged it for a chocolate truffle, knowing it would bring her grandmother joy.

As the sun began its descent, painting the skies in hues of orange and pink, Rose found herself amidst a group of children playing near a babbling brook. They were laughing and singing, their joy as infectious as the crisp autumn air. Drawing closer, she noticed a small mouse struggling to join in, hindered by a broken wheel on his toy cart. "May I help?" Rose asked kindly, her paws gently examining the damage. With a little ingenuity and a few nearby sticks, they worked together to fashion a sturdy replacement wheel. The mouse beamed, his happiness like a warm glow that spread through the group, magnifying their laughter and joy.

As evening cloaked the kingdom in twilight, the villagers gathered around a bonfire that danced with warmth and light. Rose was invited to share her day’s adventures, and she did so with a heart full of gratitude. Her tales sparked stories from others, weaving a tapestry of experiences into the cool night air. Each story was another thread in the fabric of the kingdom's rich and vibrant history, a testament to the power of kindness in all its forms. The villagers’ faces glowed in the firelight, their eyes brimming with warmth, and Rose felt a deep sense of belonging that filled every corner of her heart.

Soon, it was time to return to Kindsville. Rose bid farewell to her new friends, promising to carry the lessons of kindness with her always. As she crossed back over the rainbow bridge, the colors shimmered brighter, a path painted by kindness and love. Arriving home, Rose was greeted with open arms. She shared her clay pot with her grandmother, who smiled and hugged Rose tightly, eyes glistening with happy tears. That night, as moonlight spilled across her bed, Rose dreamed of Kindness Kingdom and woke with the sun, her heart forever blooming with the seeds of kindness she would continue to plant. THE END

books.title: Shapes in the City
books.description: Discover shapes hiding everywhere in the city.

pages.text:
Shapes in the City

Finding Shapes Everywhere!
Shelly the Circle loved rolling through the city. "I'm everywhere!"
"Look! I'm in the sun, in pizzas, in coins!" Shelly spun happily.
Sammy the Square was proud too. "Buildings need me!"
"Windows, boxes, tiles - I make things strong and neat!"
Trixie the Triangle climbed high. "I'm on top of everything!"
"Rooftops, pizza slices, mountains - I reach for the sky!"
"Let's work together!" they said. And they built amazing things!
Houses, cars, parks - all made from shapes working as friends.

Now look around YOU! What shapes can you find?

The End

books.title: The Feelings Garden
books.description: Flowers represent different emotions children can learn about.

pages.text_content: The garden existed in a place that was not quite a place — accessible through a gate in the back of an old library that should have opened into a car park but instead opened onto a path, and down the path to a garden enclosed by walls so old they had moss growing on the moss. The gardener was always there, always busy, wearing no particular expression that could be read as age. He had tended this garden for a very long time. The garden grew feelings, which was unusual but not — once you had spent time there — surprising. Things that grow need tending. Feelings, the gardener held, were no different.

Iris found the gate at age ten by following a cat through the library that turned out not to be in the library's official animal policy. She stepped through the gate and stopped. The garden was large — much larger than the car park she had been expecting — and arranged in sections, each growing different flowers. She could identify some of them in the ordinary way: sunflowers, roses, violets, something white and delicate she had no name for. But they were also, simultaneously and without contradiction, other things. The sunflowers were radiantly happy. The roses were beautifully, dangerously angry. The violets were genuinely sad. She stood at the gate and felt it.

The gardener found her standing at the gate and invited her in with the matter-of-fact welcome of someone who has been receiving visitors for a very long time and is neither surprised nor particularly making an occasion of it. He showed her around — this section for joy, this for sorrow, this for the complicated feelings that don't have simple names. He explained that the flowers grew from seeds that people brought, knowingly or not, and that tending them was important because feelings left untended could become overgrown or withered or invasive. She asked if she could help. He handed her a watering can.

The watering can was heavier than it looked and the water inside it was not quite water — it had a quality of attention to it, a sense of being noticed. She watered the section the gardener indicated: a patch of small blue flowers that were, she understood without being told, loneliness. They were delicate and needed careful watering — too much and they would drown, too little and they would wither. She watered them with the focused care of someone who understood, instinctively, that this mattered. When she finished, the flowers seemed slightly less lonely. She wasn't sure how she knew this but she did.

She came back every week after that, always on Saturday, always through the same gate. The gardener taught her the names of the feelings and the flowers that grew them and the particular care each one required. Anger needed pruning — left alone it would spread and choke other things. Fear needed sunlight and open space around it. Grief needed time and patience and the understanding that it would bloom in its own season. Love, surprisingly, was one of the hardiest plants in the garden — it could survive almost anything, though it grew best when tended regularly.

The section she found hardest to tend was shame. The flowers there were small and grew close to the ground, almost hidden, and they flinched when she approached — actually flinched, pulling their petals inward. The gardener told her that shame was the most difficult feeling to care for because it didn't want to be seen, and yet being seen with kindness was exactly what it needed. She learned to approach it slowly, to sit near it without demanding anything, to let it unfurl in its own time. It took three months before the shame flowers would let her water them properly.

She was twelve when she planted her first seed. She had been carrying something for weeks — a feeling she couldn't name, heavy and complicated, related to a friendship that had ended badly — and the gardener suggested she might want to give it somewhere to grow rather than carrying it around. She dug a small hole in a section reserved for new plantings, placed the feeling there (she didn't know how she did this, only that she did), and covered it with soil. A week later a small shoot emerged. She didn't know what it would become yet. Neither, apparently, did it.

The plant that grew from her seed took six months to flower. When it did, it was unlike anything else in the garden — not a single feeling but several intertwined: loss and love and anger and something that might have been forgiveness, all growing from the same root system, all part of the same complicated thing. The gardener looked at it for a long time and then said: 'This is rare. Most people's complicated feelings stay complicated. Yours has found a way to be complicated and whole at the same time.' She wasn't sure if this was a compliment but she decided to take it as one.

She was fourteen when she started bringing others to the garden. Friends who were struggling, who needed somewhere to put things they couldn't carry, who needed to see that feelings could be tended rather than just endured. The gardener welcomed each one with the same matter-of-fact hospitality. Some came once and never returned. Some came regularly. One stayed and became, like Iris, an apprentice — learning the names and the care and the patient work of helping things grow. The garden, she understood now, was not just a place. It was a practice.

Years later, when asked what she did, she would say she was a gardener. This was true in multiple senses. She tended a garden that most people couldn't find, through a gate in the back of a library, where feelings grew in flowers and needed the same care as any living thing. She also tended the feelings of people who came to her — not fixing them, not solving them, just helping them find somewhere to grow, giving them water and light and time. The gardener had retired by then, or moved on, or whatever gardeners like him did. The garden was hers now. She opened the gate each morning and walked through. There was always work to do. THE END

books.title: Bedtime in the Animal World
books.description: How do different animals say goodnight?

pages.text:
Bedtime in the Animal World

Time to Sleep
pages.text_content: As the golden sun dipped behind the hills, the sky transformed into a patchwork of pinks and purples, casting a cozy glow across the Animal World. Beneath the leafy canopy, a gentle hush spread through the trees, like a soft blanket rolled out for the night. Tiny eyes twinkled like stars as the forest creatures listened to the calming chorus of crickets, their rhythmic chirps a lullaby for weary ears. In the warmth of the evening air, little critters snuggled into their nests and burrows, their fur and feathers ruffled from a day of play. Each animal felt the drowsy embrace of bedtime, hearts slowing and breathing in sync with the whispered rustle of the leaves. They savored the sweet scent of blooming night flowers, a promise of dreams to come, and nestled close, welcoming the gentle arrival of a peaceful slumber.

pages.text: When the sun sets, animals everywhere get ready for bed.
pages.text_content: As the golden sun dipped gently behind the hills, its last rays painted the sky in soft hues of pink and purple. A quiet hush fell over the forest, where the trees whispered their goodnight secrets to one another. Birds fluttered back to their nests, their feathers rustling in the cool evening breeze. Down below, mice scurried into their cozy burrows, their tiny hearts warmed by the soft, furry comfort of their families close by. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming night flowers, offering a soothing aroma that signaled bedtime was near. Even the frogs at the pond slowed their playful splash and settled into stillness, feeling the gentle touch of the night air on their smooth, little backs. All around, the animals prepared to drift into dreams, feeling safe and snug as the starry night covered them with its sparkling, twinkling blanket.

pages.text: Baby bears snuggle in their warm dens. "Good night, mama bear."
pages.text_content: In the cozy corner of the dark forest, baby bears nestled beside their mama, wrapped in a cocoon of warmth and love. The den, a snug burrow tucked beneath ancient trees, was a comforting hideaway where the gentle rise and fall of Mama Bear’s belly felt like the ocean's tide. Outside, the whispering winds carried the soft songs of nearby owls, and the silvery moonlight painted delicate shadows on the den's earthy walls. The little bears, with fur as soft as the autumn leaves, felt the soothing rhythm of the night lull them into a peaceful slumber. Safe and snug, their sleepy eyes blinked slowly, and a feeling of pure contentment filled their hearts. The tiny cubs knew, under Mama's watchful gaze, their dreams would be as sweet and cozy as the home they snuggled in.

pages.text: Little owls wake up! Bedtime for them is when WE wake up!
pages.text_content: As the moon hung like a glowing lantern in the deep, velvet sky, the little owls began to stir in their snug nests high up in the whispering trees. Their big, round eyes blinked open, shimmering like marbles catching the moonlight. They fluffed their downy feathers, feeling the cool, night breeze tickle their wings. Down below, the world seemed to tiptoe as most animals snuggled into sleepy dreams. The daytime creatures had wrapped themselves in cozy dreams, while the owls, with a gentle rustling sound, stretched into their night-time adventure. A sprinkle of stars twinkled above, casting a gentle glow around them, like tiny fireflies dancing. The owls felt alive and cheerful, ready to flap and flutter into the night, bobbing on their branches as crickets serenaded them with their rhythmic chirps. For them, an exciting world awaited with mysteries under the star-speckled sky.

pages.text: Bunnies hop to their burrows. Soft grass makes the best beds!
pages.text_content: As twilight casts a gentle violet glow over the meadow, a group of fluffy bunnies with twitching noses and cotton tails bounce toward the cool safety of their burrows. The evening air carries the whisper of rustling leaves and the sweet scent of wildflowers, creating a lullaby for tired ears. Each bunny pauses, their little hearts filled with the soft drumbeat of home, as they nestle into their beds made of lush, green grass. The grass tickles their fur, like a mother’s soft hand, and wraps them in comfort. The bunnies close their eyes, feeling the gentle rise and fall of their family clustered nearby. Their minds drift to dreams of meadow adventures, while the crickets sing a sleepy serenade just for them. Bathed in starlight, the world feels wonderfully peaceful, and the bunnies drift into slumber beneath the twinkling sky.

pages.text: Fish rest in quiet waters. Even the ocean gets sleepy.
pages.text_content: As the shimmering sun dips slowly beyond the horizon, the ocean waves become gentle whispers under a blanket of twilight. Within this vast water world, colorful fish pause their playful journey, floating like glimmers of silver in the tranquil sea. The water cradles them softly, and they feel the cool, silky touch of the ocean's embrace. The once lively coral cities are now still, a place of soft shadows where the fish find their cozy hiding spots. Here, some rest above swaying seaweed, while others find calm in watery caves. Tiny bubbles rise silently, adding to the sleepy melody of the deep. The fish feel the gentle heartbeat of the ocean, steady and soothing. As the last streaks of sunlight wave goodbye, the fish close their eyes, feeling safe and snug, wrapped in the peaceful whisper of the sleepy sea.

pages.text: Puppies curl up in balls. Their paws twitch - they're dreaming!
pages.text_content: In a cozy corner of the room, the puppies nestle close, their tiny bodies snug against each other, forming soft, furry mounds on the warm, patchwork blanket. Their eyes are gently closed, eyelashes casting shadows on their velvety cheeks. Around them, a gentle hush blankets the room, broken only by the soft sighs of their sleepy snores. In their dreams, they chase the playful rays of sunshine, their paws twitching in delight as imaginary butterflies flit around their noses. The scent of fresh grass lingers in their dreams, tickling their senses with promises of adventure. Each joyful twitch of a paw hints at a world of wagging tails and wiggling noses, filled with happiness and infinite warmth. The puppies dream on, feeling safe, loved, and utterly content—ready for the adventures only dreamland can offer.

pages.text: Kittens purr and stretch. They've played hard and now they rest.
pages.text_content: Under the cozy glow of the moonlit room, the kittens lie sprawled on a soft, patterned quilt. Their tiny paws, pink and delicate like petal blossoms, twitch as they settle in. You can hear the gentle hum of their purring, a soft melody that fills the night air, wrapping around them like a warm, snug blanket. Their bellies rise and fall slowly, their breathing quiet and peaceful. After a day filled with chasing fluttering butterflies and rolling in crunchy leaves under a golden sun, the kittens feel a delightful drowsiness wash over them, like a gentle wave lulling them to sleep. With one last languid stretch, their tails curling toward the sky, they nestle into their comforting bed, their hearts full of happiness and their dreams just waiting to unfold in the starry night.

pages.text: Birds tuck heads under wings. The nest is quiet and warm.
pages.text_content: As the soft glow of the moon filters through the leafy branches, birds in their fluffy nests begin to settle in for the night. Tiny sparrows flutter their feathers and nuzzle close, each one finding comfort as they tuck their little heads beneath their wings. The nest, woven snugly with twigs and leaves, cradles them like a gentle hug. From above, a cooling night breeze whispers through the trees, yet inside the nest, it is warm and peaceful. The rhythmic chirping of crickets dances through the forest, creating a soothing lullaby that lulls the birds into sleepy contentment. Their eyes slowly droop, heavy with dreams of tomorrow's sunny skies and flitting through meadows of flowers. An overwhelming sense of safety wraps around them, as if the whole world has paused for their slumber. It is truly bedtime in the animal kingdom.

pages.text:
And somewhere, a little one like YOU is getting sleepy too. Sweet dreams!

The End
pages.text_content: Under the vast, star-speckled sky, beneath a blanket of twinkling constellations, a soft whisper like a lullaby floats through the gentle night air. Somewhere in the cozy glow of a child's room, a little one like YOU snuggles beneath a toasty quilt, feeling its warmth wrap them like a hug. The velvety shadows dance across the walls, casting playful, dreamlike shapes that sway and stretch, inviting your imagination to wander in magical lands. Outside, the night hush sings the hushed song of crickets as the cool breeze lightly tickles the trees. Your eyelashes grow heavy, slowly drifting down like sleepy butterflies finding a place to rest. The world becomes a gentle murmur, and with each soft breath, comfort and peace wrap around you. Sweet dreams await, as the night carefully tucks you in, where adventures fill your slumber until the morning sun arrives.

books.title: Flame's Courageous Journey
books.description: An enchanting tale about a small dragon named Flame who learns to conquer his fear of fire with the help of a wise owl.
books.back_cover_text: Join Flame, a little dragon with a big heart, on an adventure to find his inner strength. With the guidance of a wise owl named Ollie, Flame discovers that bravery means facing your fears and learning from them.

pages.text: Deep in the heart of the Elderwood Forest, where the trees grew so tall their tops disappeared into the clouds, there lived a small dragon named Flame. He had emerald green scales, wings the colour of autumn leaves, and a tail that curled up at the end like a question mark. The other young dragons spent their days breathing fire at logs, scorching patterns into the bark, and competing to see who could make the biggest flame. But Flame always watched from a safe distance, his belly tight with a feeling he could not quite name. The truth was — and it was a truth that filled him with great shame — Flame was afraid of fire.

One quiet afternoon, Flame sat alone on a mossy rock at the edge of a stream, watching his reflection in the water and wondering if there was something terribly wrong with him. That was when Ollie landed on the branch above. Ollie was the oldest owl in the forest, with wide amber eyes and feathers so soft he made almost no sound when he flew. He tilted his head and studied Flame for a long moment. 'You have the expression of someone carrying a very heavy stone,' Ollie observed. Flame looked up, startled. He thought about denying it, but Ollie's eyes were kind. 'I am afraid of fire,' Flame admitted at last, in barely more than a whisper. 'And I am a dragon. So what does that make me?' He braced himself for laughter. But Ollie did not laugh at all.

'It makes you honest,' said Ollie calmly. 'Most creatures spend their whole lives being afraid of things but pretending they are not. You have already done something brave — you have named it.' He spread his great wings and glided down to sit beside Flame on the rock. 'Fear is not a wall,' Ollie continued. 'It is a door. And doors can be opened.' He told Flame that he knew a place deep in the forest where small, gentle fires burned in the roots of the ancient trees — fires that had burned quietly for a thousand years, hurting nothing, warming everything around them. Together, they set off through the shadowy ferns, Flame's heart hammering with every step.

The ancient fires were nothing like what Flame had imagined. They were not roaring or violent or hungry. They were small and still, burning in little cups of stone among the tree roots, as steady and calm as breathing. Their light was warm gold, and the air around them smelled of pine and something older and sweeter that Flame had no word for. Ollie said nothing. He simply waited. After a long time, Flame leaned forward and blew — the gentlest breath he had ever taken. A tiny flame appeared at the tip of his tongue. It danced for a moment in the air, then joined the fire in the stone cup, adding its small light to the larger warmth. Flame stared at what he had done. 'I did it,' he said, barely believing it. Ollie's eyes crinkled with quiet joy.

On the way home through the forest, Flame felt different — not because the fear had completely gone, but because he had looked at it clearly and taken one small step toward it anyway. He thought about what Ollie had said: that bravery was not the absence of fear, but moving forward while the fear was still there. When the other dragons saw him the next day and invited him to join their fire-breathing games, Flame took a deep breath and stepped forward. His flame was small and gentle — nothing like the great blazing roars of his friends. But it was real, and it was his, and as he watched it curl upward into the morning air, Flame felt something in his chest that was warm in a completely different way from fire. He felt proud.
Big dragons couldn't help - their fire made steam that made things worse!
But Flame had an idea! His tiny sparks could light the warning beacons!
One by one, Flame lit every beacon. The village was warned in time!
"You saved us all!" the villagers cheered. Flame stood tall with pride.

Flame learned that being different isn't bad - it's what makes you special!

The End

books.title: Luna's Rainbow Adventure
books.description: Join young astronaut Luna as she discovers a moon of rainbow crystals and meets a civilization of friendly aliens, embarking on a delightful journey of friendship and wonder.
books.back_cover_text: Luna the astronaut lands on a sparkly moon! Meet her new friends from a cheerful alien civilization and explore the dazzling world of rainbow crystals. Adventure and friendship await!

pages.text: Luna had always dreamed of exploring the stars. She had spent her whole childhood lying in the grass outside her house, watching the night sky and pointing at distant lights and wondering what they felt like up close. So when she grew up and became an astronaut — a real one, with a silver suit and a helmet that reflected the whole world back at her — it felt less like a new beginning and more like finally arriving somewhere she had always been going. On a bright Tuesday morning, her spacecraft hummed to life and carried her away from everything she knew, out into the deep, velvet dark. Her mission was to survey a newly discovered moon — one that the scientists back home had given a long number as a name, but which Luna, the moment she saw it glimmering on her monitor, privately called Rainbow.

When the spacecraft landed with a soft crunch and Luna stepped out onto the surface, she stood completely still for a long moment. The ground beneath her boots was made of something she had no word for — not rock exactly, not sand, but something in between, and it caught the light of the distant sun and threw it back in fragments of every colour imaginable. Wherever she looked, the surface sparkled. Pinks and greens and deep purples and flashing golds. The scientists had told her the moon was made of a type of mineral crystal that refracted light, but no description had prepared her for this — for the feeling of standing in the middle of so much impossible beauty. She turned slowly on the spot, mouth open inside her helmet, breathing too fast.

She was still standing there, turning slowly, when she heard something she definitely had not expected: laughter. It was light and bubbling, like water over stones, and it seemed to be coming from behind a cluster of tall crystal formations nearby. Luna checked her equipment — all readings normal, atmosphere not breathable, no signs of life on any scanner. And yet. The laughter came again. She took a breath, squared her shoulders, and walked toward it. Around the edge of the crystals, she stopped dead. Standing in a loose, cheerful group were creatures unlike anything she had ever seen or imagined. They were small — about the height of her knee — with large round eyes that shimmered with every colour of the surface beneath their feet. They were looking at her with enormous curiosity and, it seemed, considerable delight.

They communicated not in words but in gestures and colours — the shimmering of their eyes, the movement of their small hands, patterns that rippled across their skin like light through water. Luna, who had trained for years for contact with alien life and had privately assumed it would be formal and terrifying, found herself simply smiling. One of them — the smallest, with eyes that flickered between deep blue and warm gold — stepped forward and took her gloved hand with both of its tiny ones and held it. That was the introduction. Luna named them the Crystal Friends, because she needed to call them something, and they seemed to understand that too, tilting their heads and repeating the sound back to her in high, bright tones.

For the rest of the day, they showed her everything. She learned that the crystals sang — a low, barely audible vibration that changed pitch with the temperature, a constant music that the Crystal Friends had grown up listening to. She learned that their colours shifted with their feelings: deep blue when they were calm, bright yellow when excited, soft pink when they were being kind. She watched them play — a game that involved rolling smooth pebbles across the crystal ground and watching the light scatter in different patterns — and found herself laughing along, even when she did not fully understand the rules. By the time the distant sun began to set, painting the whole moon in extraordinary shades of amber and violet, Luna felt as though she had known them for years.

When her instruments told her it was time to return to the spacecraft, Luna felt a tightness in her chest that she had not expected. She turned to the Crystal Friends and pressed both hands over her heart — the universal gesture she had improvised for 'I am glad I met you' — and they responded by pressing their own hands over their hearts and then reaching them toward her, palms open. She walked backward toward the ship, not wanting to turn away until she absolutely had to. As the spacecraft rose from the glittering surface and the moon grew small below her, Luna pressed her hand against the viewport. She had promised, in the only way she could, that she would come back. And as the little moon sparkled in the darkness behind her, she was already thinking about how.
Green took her to a jungle planet with talking trees!
Blue brought her to an ocean world with flying fish!
Purple led to a quiet world where dreams are made.

Home on the full rainbow! Luna knew she'd visit again.

The End

books.title: Lila and the Whispering Blossoms
books.description: Lila, a shy forest fairy, finds her special gift and learns the beauty of friendship with woodland creatures.
books.back_cover_text: Join Lila, the timid forest fairy, as she discovers her magical ability to speak with flowers. With the help of her newfound woodland friends, Lila learns the courage to embrace her own special gift.

pages.text: Deep in the heart of the Glimmering Woodlands, where sunlight filtered through leaves in long golden shafts and the air always smelled of rain and honey, there lived a small fairy named Lila. She had hair the colour of copper and wings like a dragonfly — translucent and shot through with little rainbows when the light caught them just right. Lila loved the forest with her whole heart. She loved the sound of the stream and the feeling of soft moss underfoot and the way the older trees seemed to breathe slowly in the dark. But whenever she came across another woodland creature — a hedgehog, a robin, a young fox — she would freeze up completely, her wings pressing flat against her back, and find she had nothing at all to say. She was, in the most gentle and private way, terribly shy.
pages.text_content: In a sun-drenched garden at the edge of a quiet village, there lived a little girl named Lila. She had warm brown hair and big, curious eyes, and she spent every afternoon wandering among the flowers. The roses, the daisies, the tall orange birds of paradise — Lila knew every one of them by heart. A little robin often perched nearby, watching her with its bright black eyes as she walked the paths alone. Lila was the kind of girl who noticed small things. She noticed the way petals caught the light. She noticed the way the garden smelled just before rain. And one afternoon, she noticed something else — something quite extraordinary.

pages.text: One sunny morning, while Lila was sitting very quietly near a cluster of white flowers, she heard something that made her sit bolt upright. A voice — tiny and bright and unmistakably cheerful — said: 'Hello there!' Lila spun around, wings snapping open in surprise. There was nobody behind her. Nobody above her. Nobody to the left or right. She looked down at the flowers. One of them — a small white blossom with a golden centre — had turned ever so slightly toward her. 'Was that... you?' Lila whispered. The flower's petals ruffled, and she was almost certain it was nodding. 'I have been watching you sit here for three mornings,' the flower said. 'I thought it was time we were introduced.'
pages.text_content: Lila was crouching beside a tall pink flower when it happened. The flower tilted its head toward her — just slightly, just enough — and said in a small, bright voice: 'Hello there!' Lila stumbled backward in surprise. She looked left and right. There was no one else in the garden. Slowly, she leaned back toward the flower. 'Was that... you?' she whispered. The flower's petals trembled, and Lila was quite certain it was nodding. 'We have always been able to talk,' it said cheerfully. 'Most people simply walk past too quickly to hear. But you always stop. You always look. So today, we thought it was time to say hello properly.'

pages.text: Lila's first thought was that she must be dreaming. Her second thought was that if she was dreaming, she might as well enjoy it. She leaned closer. 'Can all flowers talk?' she asked. 'Oh, we always could,' the blossom said cheerfully. 'Most people simply do not know how to listen. You are quieter than most, and quiet is the right kind of listening.' Over the next hour, Lila sat in absolute wonder as the flowers told her things she had never known — which paths led to the sweetest berries, where the foxes went in winter, why the great oak at the forest's heart had a hollow big enough to sleep in. The forest she thought she knew was full of secrets she had never even guessed at.
pages.text_content: Lila laughed — a real laugh, bright and surprised, the kind that made her spin on the spot with her arms out. The flowers laughed too, in their own way, their petals trembling with delight. 'Can all of you talk?' she asked, looking around at the whole garden. 'Every one of us,' said a cheerful daisy nearby. 'We have been waiting for someone quiet enough to listen.' That afternoon, Lila sat in the middle of the garden and the flowers told her everything — which paths led to the sweetest wild berries, where the foxes made their dens at the edge of the wood, why the old oak tree at the far wall had a hollow just the right size to keep a secret.

pages.text: That afternoon, filled with more courage than she had felt in a long time, Lila flew to find the other woodland creatures. She found the hedgehog first, snuffling through the leaves near the brook. 'Excuse me,' Lila said, her voice barely louder than the rustling leaves. 'The flowers told me you know where the very best mushrooms grow. I thought perhaps you might like to show me?' The hedgehog looked up, surprised that anyone had spoken to him so gently. 'I would like that very much,' he said. Word spread, the way words do in a forest, and by evening a small gathering had formed around the flower patch — a robin, two young rabbits, a sleepy dormouse, and even a cautious young deer standing at the edge of the clearing.
pages.text_content: With her heart full of new courage, Lila decided to find the other creatures of the garden and share what she had learned. She found a small white rabbit first, sitting very still among the pink blooms. 'Excuse me,' said Lila softly, kneeling down so she was at his level. 'The flowers told me you know all the best hiding places in this garden. I thought perhaps you would like to show me?' The rabbit looked up at her with round dark eyes. He had not expected anyone to speak to him so gently. 'I would like that very much,' he said quietly. 'I have been sitting here alone for quite a long time.' And so they set off together, following the flower-lined paths through the afternoon light.

pages.text: Lila stood in the middle of them all — the creatures she had watched from a distance for so long — and felt something open up inside her like a flower itself. She introduced each creature to the flowers, who greeted everyone warmly. She translated the flowers' stories for those who could not quite hear them. She laughed for the first time in what felt like months. And as the sun dipped below the trees and painted the clearing amber and rose, Lila realised that her shyness had not disappeared — it was still there, soft and familiar — but it had made room for something else. The most magical gift, she thought, as the flowers whispered goodnight, was not the ability to hear them at all. It was finding out that she had been worth talking to all along.
pages.text_content: Word spread through the garden the way it does when something good is happening — quickly, warmly, without anyone quite knowing how it started. By the time the sun was beginning to dip, Lila found herself surrounded. There were butterflies resting on her shoulders. There were bees hovering nearby in contented circles. There were tiny birds she had never seen before, watching from the branches above with tilted heads. And the flowers were talking all at once, telling stories and asking questions and laughing their petal-trembling laugh. Lila stood in the middle of it all and felt something she had not felt in a long time — not just happy, but completely, entirely at home. She had been coming to this garden every day for years. Today, for the first time, it had welcomed her back.

pages.text: "What do you need?" Lila whispered. "Someone to sing to me."
pages.text_content: As the afternoon grew late, Lila came upon a part of the garden she had never explored — a quiet corner behind the tall roses, where a girl stood alone among the flowers. She was taller than Lila, with long brown hair and a small golden crown that caught the slanting light. She looked proud, but also somehow sad. When she saw Lila, she did not speak. She simply looked at her with very serious eyes. 'Hello,' said Lila carefully. 'I did not know anyone else came here.' The girl with the crown was quiet for a long moment. Then she said, very softly: 'What do you need?' Lila blinked. 'I don't need anything,' she said. 'I am just happy being here.' The girl's expression shifted — something in it softened. 'Someone to sing to me,' she finally admitted. 'That is what I need.'

pages.text: Lila sang her grandmother's lullaby, soft and sweet.
pages.text_content: Lila thought for a moment. Then she remembered the song her grandmother used to sing on summer evenings — a gentle, lilting melody with no particular words, just a rise and fall like breathing. She opened her mouth and sang it, softly at first, then more fully as her voice found its shape. Something extraordinary happened. As Lila sang, tiny pink butterflies appeared — first one, then three, then dozens — rising from the flowers around her feet in a soft, spiralling cloud. They drifted upward into the golden light, turning slow, lazy circles above the garden, their wings catching the sun like rose-coloured sparks. Lila sang and sang. The butterflies rose and rose. And the girl with the crown stood very still and listened with her eyes closed, and the tightness around her mouth slowly, gently eased away.

pages.text: The Queen Blossom stood tall again! Her petals glowed!
pages.text_content: When Lila finished singing, the garden was very quiet. Then, from the corner of the garden, came a sound — a deep, slow sound like a breath being released after a very long time. The Queen Blossom, the oldest and largest flower in the whole garden, who had been drooping for weeks with her petals turned toward the ground, lifted her great pink head. Her petals opened wide. They did not just open — they glowed, softly, from within, like a lantern lit against the evening. 'Thank you,' said the Queen Blossom, in a voice that seemed to come from the roots of the earth itself. 'I had forgotten that song.' Lila held the small blossom the Queen offered her and felt its warmth pulse gently in her palm, like a tiny heartbeat.

pages.text: "Thank you, little one. Music heals the soul - even flower souls."
pages.text_content: The girl with the crown knelt down beside the Queen Blossom and touched one of her glowing petals very carefully. Then she looked at Lila. 'How did you know what to do?' she asked. Lila thought about it honestly. 'I didn't,' she said. 'I just did what felt right.' She held out the small heart-shaped flower that had appeared in her hand, and offered it to the girl. 'I think this is for you,' Lila said. 'I think the garden wanted you to have it.' The girl took it with both hands, the way you take something precious. 'Thank you, little one,' she said quietly. 'Music heals the soul. Even flower souls.' She looked around at the glowing, breathing garden and for the first time since Lila had met her, she smiled.

pages.text:
Now Lila sings to her garden every day. And it sings back!

The End
pages.text_content: After that day, Lila came to the garden every morning without fail. She brought her singing voice with her the way other children bring toys or books. She sang to the roses when they were drooping. She sang to the seedlings when they were just beginning to push through the soil. She sang to the butterflies and the bees and the little birds in the branches above. And every time she sang, the garden sang back — in its own way, with the rustle of leaves and the turning of petals and the soft, warm sound of everything growing. Lila had come to the garden looking for nothing in particular. She had found something she had not known she was looking for. And now Lila sings to her garden every day. And it sings back. The End.

books.title: The Midnight Brush
books.description: A magical tale of a young artist whose paintings come alive each night, leading to a colorful and enchanting adventure.
books.back_cover_text: Join Emma on a whimsical journey as her painted friends come to life after dark. With her creativity and courage, she must help them find their way back to their homes before sunrise!

pages.text: Emma's bedroom was more art studio than bedroom, which her parents had accepted with the philosophical grace of people who had tried the alternative and found it did not work. Her bed was pushed into one corner to make room for the easel. The windowsill was lined with jars of brushes and stained, beloved palettes. The walls — where they were visible beneath the canvases that covered almost every surface — were a pale cream that the paint had long since found its way to in interesting patterns. Emma painted every evening after school and sometimes in the morning before, and she painted with the particular focus of someone who had found the thing they were meant to do and was simply getting on with doing it. She was eleven years old and she had never once had to think about what to do with her hands. Colours talked to her in a way she found difficult to describe but never needed to explain — she simply knew, always, which one came next.

The first time it happened, Emma thought she was dreaming. She had fallen asleep at her desk — not unusual — and woken to find the studio lit by a different kind of light than the moon, warmer and more golden, and the painting on the easel in front of her was moving. Not violently or strangely — the bird in the upper left corner was simply flying, its wings rising and falling with the easy authority of real flight. And then it banked toward her and landed on the edge of the frame, and looked at her with painted eyes that were somehow entirely alive. 'Hello,' it said, in a voice like rustling leaves. Before she could speak, a low sound behind her made her turn: the lion from the large canvas on the wall had stepped forward until his front paws rested on the baseboard, his golden eyes steady. 'We've been waiting for the right night,' the lion said. 'We need your help.'

They explained carefully. Each of them — the bird, the lion, and gradually others who stepped forward from their canvases and found space in the small room — had been painted into a world. A beautiful world, a world Emma had made with love and care and the particular attention she brought to everything she painted. But they were, they told her, not quite home. 'You painted us well,' the bird said, perched on her shoulder now, its painted feathers surprisingly soft. 'But the world we come from is beyond what you can see. We need a path.' Emma looked at the lion, who had settled onto the rug with the quiet confidence of something that had always belonged there. She thought for a moment, then she reached for her brushes. 'Tell me what it looks like,' she said. 'The place you're trying to get back to. Tell me every detail.'

She painted through the night, listening to their descriptions — the colours of their sky, the particular quality of the light in their home places, the sounds that came at dawn. The wise old tree from the large landscape painting in the corner joined them at some point, its bark-textured voice rolling slowly through the room, offering observations about direction and season that Emma found she could translate directly into colour and angle of light. She painted a path — not a literal road but something more like a memory of one, shimmering at the edges where the possible met the definite. She painted the horizon they described with such care that she found herself half-believing in it herself. As she worked, the room filled with the smell of somewhere else — salt air and pine and warm stone — that she knew was not coming from her paints.

Just before dawn — the sky outside beginning to shift from deep blue to grey — Emma stood back from the canvas and looked at what she had made. The path gleamed softly on the surface, leading from a point near the bottom right of the image toward the upper left, disappearing into a light that she had not consciously decided to paint but that felt exactly right. The bird flew to the path first, circling it once, and then moved into it and was gone — not dramatically, not with any flourish, just gone, in the way that things go when they arrive at exactly where they were always going. The lion followed, slower, and paused at the edge to look back at Emma with an expression she could not describe but would remember for the rest of her life. The others followed one by one, until the room was quiet. Emma stood alone in her studio as the sun came up and turned everything gold, and she understood, with the deep, calm certainty of someone who has done something exactly right, that this was why she painted. THE END
He painted a dragon - friendly, of course! They flew over the town.
But then he painted something sad - a lonely monster.
"I don't want to be scary," it cried. So Milo painted it a friend!
He learned: what you create affects others. Paint with kindness!

Now Milo only paints joy. And every midnight, his room fills with friends.

The End

books.title: The Emotion Squad: Power of Unity
books.description: Join the adventure of the Emotion Squad, a group of young superheroes who discover the true power of friendship and teamwork through their emotion-based abilities.
books.cover_title: The Emotion Squad: Power of Unity
books.back_cover_text: Meet the Emotion Squad, young superheroes with powers driven by their feelings. When a mysterious force threatens their town, they learn that working together brings their strongest magic to life. Can they unite to save the day?

pages.text: The town of Cheerstone sat in a sunny valley between two gentle hills, and it was, by any measure, a happy place. The streets were wide and clean, the park had excellent swings, and the bakery on the corner always seemed to be producing something that smelled wonderful. But the most remarkable thing about Cheerstone was not any of this. It was five children who lived there — children who, for reasons that nobody had ever fully explained, had grown up with something extra. Joy could make flowers grow with her laughter and could lift the spirits of anyone within earshot of her voice. Calm moved through difficult situations like water around stones, never getting caught up, always finding the steadiest path. Brave felt fear just like everyone else but had somehow never let it win. Kind noticed things — small things, the specific things — that others missed entirely. And Creative could look at any problem sideways and find a solution where none seemed to exist. They had called themselves, with characteristic directness, the Emotion Squad.

It began on a Thursday morning with a shadow. Not the ordinary shadow that a cloud casts — this was something different, something that settled over the town with a weight to it, that made the light feel thinner and the colours less vivid. By afternoon, people in Cheerstone were moving more slowly than usual, speaking more quietly, stopping in the middle of sentences as though they had forgotten what they meant to say. The birds in the park went quiet. The bakery closed early. Joy, who felt changes in mood the way other people felt changes in temperature, noticed it first — a shift in the emotional weather of the whole town that made her stomach tighten. She sent a message to the others and they gathered at their usual meeting place: the old bandstand at the centre of the park, which they had claimed as their base of operations three summers ago and had never officially given up.

They could see the cloud from the bandstand — it sat above the eastern part of town, dark and still, not moving with the wind the way a normal cloud should. 'I'll try first,' Joy said, and she took a breath and laughed — her full laugh, the one that usually sent flowers exploding into bloom across the grass. For a moment, a shaft of sunlight broke through the cloud and the townspeople below looked up, blinking, and smiled. But the cloud reformed. The light disappeared. The shadow deepened. Brave went next, flying straight up at the cloud with her arms wide and her face set with determination — and for a few seconds the cloud wavered and the shadows receded. But it held. Kind tried talking to it, which was not as strange as it sounded — Kind could often reach things that others couldn't by simply acknowledging them. The cloud rumbled but didn't move. One by one, each of them tried everything they knew, and each time the cloud came back.

It was Creative who said, quietly, what all of them were already beginning to think. 'We keep trying to fix it alone,' she said. 'We each go in with our own thing and the cloud absorbs it and closes up again. But what if—' she paused, working it out as she spoke, which was how her best ideas always arrived, 'what if the reason it keeps coming back is because it's bigger than any one of us? What if it needs all of us at once?' They looked at each other. It was obvious, put that way. So obvious that Brave said 'Why didn't we think of that before?' and Calm said 'We were too busy doing to see it,' which was, they all felt, probably true. They moved to stand in a circle — Joy, Calm, Brave, Kind, Creative — and they each reached out until their hands met, and they each brought with them, completely and without holding back, everything that they were.

What rose from their joined hands was not any one colour. It was all of them at once — warm gold and cool blue and steady green and bright rose and the particular kind of silver-white that belongs to possibility. It rose in a column toward the cloud and hit it not like an attack but like an opening — the way a window lets in light not by force but by simply being present. The cloud shuddered. For a moment it seemed to pull tighter, to resist. And then, slowly at first and then all at once, it began to break apart. Sunlight poured through. The townspeople below lifted their heads. A child in the park began to run just for the pleasure of it. The baker opened her shutters and the smell of cinnamon rolled down the street. The birds started again. The five of them stood in their circle and watched the last of the shadow dissolve into the blue sky above Cheerstone and felt something that was bigger than any of their individual powers: the particular satisfaction of something that could only have been done together.

That evening they sat on the bandstand steps while the sun went down and painted the valley in amber and rose, and they talked — the way they did after every difficult day — about what they had learned. 'We always go in separately first,' Brave said. 'Every time.' 'Because we each think we might be enough,' Joy said honestly. 'And sometimes one of us is,' Calm said. 'But sometimes the problem is bigger. And the hard part is knowing the difference.' Kind turned her hands over in her lap, thinking about the moment the cloud had broken. 'It was not just more power,' she said slowly. 'When we joined, it was not that we had five times as much of anything. It was something different. Something new.' Creative, who had been quiet for a while, nodded. 'That's what friendship does,' she said. 'It makes something that wasn't there before.' They watched the sun finish setting. Cheerstone glowed below them, fully itself again, warm and lit and full of the particular sound of a town that had remembered how to be happy. THE END
Calm helps us breathe and think clearly.
One day, a big problem came. Each emotion tried alone - but failed!
"Together!" said Joy. They combined their powers!

All emotions matter. Together, they make us complete!

The End

books.title: Friendship Island
books.description: Five friends get stranded on an island and learn about teamwork.
books.back_cover_text: When their boat drifts away, five friends must work together to survive on a mysterious island.

pages.text: In the middle of a wide, sparkling sea, there was a small island where two animals lived side by side. On the left side of the island lived Turtle, who moved slowly and thought carefully about everything before she did it. On the right side lived Hummingbird, who moved so fast he was often just a blur of green and arrived somewhere before he had quite decided to go there. They had lived on the island for years and years without ever once saying hello, because the island, though small, had somehow always felt just large enough for them to stay on their own sides.

One stormy morning, a great wave came and swept away Turtle's favourite flat rock, which she had sat on every single day since she could remember. She stood where it had been and felt a sadness she did not quite know what to do with. Hummingbird, zipping past overhead, stopped in mid-air and hovered. He had seen what happened. He thought about flying on. Then he thought about the sadness on Turtle's face, and he flew down instead. 'I know where there is a much better rock,' he said. 'I've seen it from the air. I could show you, if you like.' Turtle looked at him for a moment. 'I move very slowly,' she said. 'That is all right,' said Hummingbird. 'I have been moving too fast for too long. I think I could use the practice.'

They walked together across the island — or rather, Turtle walked and Hummingbird hovered beside her at walking pace, which was completely new to him. He discovered that at this speed you noticed things. The pattern the grass made in the wind. The way the sea sounded different on different parts of the shore. Turtle, for her part, discovered that having someone beside her made the same walk she had done a thousand times feel entirely different. They reached the rock — it was wider and flatter and caught the afternoon sun perfectly. Turtle stepped onto it and settled her weight. 'Yes,' she said. 'This is better.' They sat together as the sun went down and the sea turned gold, and neither of them said anything for a while, because it turned out that being comfortable in silence with someone is one of the best kinds of friendship there is. THE END
Breeze the seagull landed nearby. "Hello!" Sunny scuttled away nervously.
One stormy day, Sunny's shell collection washed away!
Splash dove deep to find the shells. Breeze flew high to spot them!
Together they brought back every single shell!
"You did that... for ME?" Sunny couldn't believe it.
"That's what friends do," Splash smiled. Sunny smiled back.

Now the island isn't lonely anymore. It's Friendship Island!

The End

pages.text_content: Isla began to look forward to checking the beach each morning more than anything else. On the days when a bottle was there, she would sit on the sand immediately and read without moving until she had finished every word. On the days when no bottle had arrived, she would sit for a while anyway, watching the direction of Leo's island, wondering what he was doing. She wrote him a letter about this and he wrote back: 'I do the same thing. I've named the gap of sea between us the Friendship Channel.' Isla thought this was the best name she had ever heard.

One letter contained a drawing — a careful, detailed map of Leo's island, with every tree and rock and the little crab pool where Pinchy lived labelled in tiny precise handwriting. Isla pinned it to the wall of her hut and looked at it every day. She drew one of her own island in return, marking the tallest coconut tree (she called it the Observatory because you could see everything from the top), the best tide pool, and the spot on the western beach where dolphins sometimes appeared at dawn.

Then came the letter Isla had been secretly hoping for. 'I have been building something,' Leo wrote. 'I am not very good at building but I have been practising. I think it might be ready in two weeks. I am going to sail to your island. I hope that is all right. Pinchy says it is a terrible idea because of the open water but Pinchy is a crab and therefore cautious by nature. Please write back and tell me where to land.' Isla wrote back immediately: 'The western beach. The dolphins will know you're a friend.'

The two weeks felt like two years. Isla cleaned her hut thoroughly. She stocked up on coconuts and dried fish. She practised conversations in her head and then felt embarrassed about practising conversations in her head. On the morning of the fourteenth day she climbed the Observatory tree before sunrise and sat there watching the horizon. The sun came up. The sea glittered. Nothing. Then, just after breakfast, a small shape appeared on the water — a raft with a patched sail, moving steadily westward.

The raft bumped onto the western beach and a boy climbed out — slightly sunburned, slightly damp, carrying a battered bag and what appeared to be a very grumpy crab in a small jar of seawater. Isla stood on the beach and they looked at each other. They had written hundreds of words to each other. Now neither of them could think of a single one. Then they both started talking at the same time, and then both stopped at the same time, and then both laughed at exactly the same moment — the same laugh, it turned out, surprised and delighted.

Leo stayed for a week. They climbed the Observatory tree together and saw four other islands from the top. They snorkelled over the reef with the red coral and Leo drew a new map with everything in it. Pinchy escaped from his jar and spent three days hiding behind the tide pool rocks before consenting to come back. They ate coconut and dried fish and talked from morning until the stars came out, catching up on all the conversations you can't have in a letter, discovering that a friend you have only written to is exactly as real as a friend you can stand next to.

When Leo sailed back to his own island, he left the map he had drawn on the wall of Isla's hut, next to the one she had drawn of his. Two islands. Two maps. A channel of sea between them that already felt like a road. That evening Isla sat on the western beach and a bottle came in on the tide — it must have been thrown just before he set sail. Inside was a note: 'Same time next month? I'll bring better provisions. Pinchy says absolutely not but we both know he doesn't mean it.' Isla laughed. She was already composing her reply. THE END

books.title: The Robot Who Wanted Friends
books.description: A lonely robot learns what it means to have friends.
books.back_cover_text: ROBO-7 was built to work, but all he wants is a friend. A heartwarming story about friendship.

pages.text: In a workshop at the end of a quiet street, a robot named Cog sat on a shelf and watched the world through a small round window. He had been built to count things — screws, bolts, measurements — and he was very good at it. But what Cog really wanted, more than anything he could count, was a friend. He watched the children playing outside his window every day and wondered what it felt like to play. He had never tried. He wasn't sure robots were allowed to try.

One afternoon, a girl with red boots and a large umbrella stopped outside the window and looked right at him. Cog went very still. People didn't usually look at him — they looked past him, at the tools on the wall or the parts on the bench. But this girl looked at him with clear, interested eyes. Then she waved. Cog had not waved before. He raised one hand, very slowly, and moved it side to side the way he had seen the children do. The girl's face broke into a wide smile. She pointed at the door. Cog looked at the door. Then he climbed down from the shelf, which took a while because his legs were quite short, and opened it.

Her name was Isla, and she was seven, and she said she had been wondering about him for weeks. They walked together to the park, which was new for Cog and interesting in many ways he had not anticipated — the grass felt strange under his metal feet, and the wind made a sound against his body that he decided he liked. Isla showed him how to play — not complicated games, just the simple ones: rolling a ball, collecting interesting leaves, counting clouds. Cog was very good at the counting part. Isla was very good at the finding part. By the end of the afternoon, when the light turned orange and Isla's mother called her home, Cog understood what playing felt like. It felt like exactly the kind of thing he had been built for all along, even though nobody had put it in his instructions. THE END
"That is friendship," the computer said. "Robots don't need it."
But Rusty WANTED it! He tried to play but didn't know how.
He brought toys - too many! He talked - too loud! Everything was wrong.
Sad Rusty sat alone. A little girl came up. "Are you okay?"
"I want friends but I don't know how," Rusty admitted.
"Just be yourself," she smiled. "And listen. That's how friendship starts."

Rusty learned to listen, share, and care. Now he has more friends than circuits!

The End

pages.text_content: He put down the bolts. He had never left the workshop before during working hours. He walked to the door, which had a handle he had never used from this side, and opened it. The outside air was different from workshop air — warmer, fuller of information. The girl was standing right there. 'I'm Bea,' she said. Her voice was friendly and direct. 'I've been watching you sort things for three weeks. You're very fast.' Cog processed this. 'I know,' he said, because it was true. 'What else can you do?' Bea asked. Cog thought about this for longer than expected. He had never been asked before.

They sat on the wall outside the workshop. Bea had a lot of questions, which Cog answered as accurately as he could. Yes, he could hear. Yes, he could see in colour. No, he didn't sleep — he had a low-power mode but it wasn't the same. Yes, he had opinions about things, though he was still developing what those were. Did he like things? He considered this. He liked when the bolts were sorted correctly. He liked the sound of rain on the workshop roof. He thought he might like talking to Bea, though he would need more data. 'That's basically how it works for me too,' said Bea. Cog found this helpful.

Bea taught him hopscotch the following Saturday. His weight distribution made it technically challenging and he left noticeable impressions in the pavement where he landed, but the principle was sound and with modifications it worked. He was considerably better at the counting aspects than the jumping aspects. Bea was considerably better at the jumping aspects. They made, she said, a good team. Cog logged this: first use of the word 'team' in relation to himself. He noted it felt different from other information. It had a quality he didn't have a processing category for yet. He created one. He labelled it: significant.

Bea introduced him to her friends one afternoon: three children from her class named Omar, Yuki, and Dev, who arrived in a group and regarded Cog with varying degrees of fascination. Omar asked him questions about his mechanics with great enthusiasm. Yuki was quieter but watched him with an attention that he recognised as the same kind he used himself. Dev immediately challenged him to a maths race, which Cog won comprehensively, and then challenged him to a drawing race, which Dev won comprehensively, and then they spent half an hour teaching each other and both improved, which Dev said was the whole point.

The thing Cog was worst at, he discovered, was understanding emotions. He could identify them — he had excellent facial recognition and he had studied body language extensively — but understanding why they happened and what they required in response was more difficult. Bea was patient about explaining. 'When someone is sad,' she said, 'you don't need to fix it. Sometimes you just stay.' Cog processed this. It went against his core programming, which was oriented toward problem-solving. 'Just stay?' he said. 'Yes,' said Bea. 'That's usually enough.' He practised staying. It turned out to require considerable effort but produced good results.

The workshop owner noticed the change in Cog. The sorting was still perfect — impeccable, as always — but Cog seemed different in a way that was hard to define. More present, perhaps. More oriented toward the window. He came in one evening to find Bea sitting on the workshop floor, doing homework, while Cog sorted next to her in companionable quiet. They weren't talking. They were just there, in the same space, being comfortable with each other. The workshop owner watched them for a moment and then quietly backed out and went home. Some things, he understood, didn't need interfering with.

One afternoon Cog told Bea something he had calculated but not said out loud: that before she had pressed her nose against his window, he had been running at approximately forty percent of his potential. Not mechanically — his sorting was always perfect. But in every other way. 'You were lonely,' Bea said. 'Yes,' said Cog. 'That is the correct word.' Bea thought about this. 'I was a bit lonely too,' she said. 'Even with people around. It's different when you find the right one.' Cog filed this carefully. He was going to need a much larger category labelled significant. THE END

books.title: Princess and the Enchanted Forest
books.description: Princess Luna discovers a magical forest full of talking animals.
books.back_cover_text: Beyond the castle walls lies a forest where animals talk and magic is real. Join Princess Luna's adventure!

pages.text: Princess Nadia had everything a princess was supposed to have — a tall tower, a kind horse, and a very nice crown that she kept polishing because it helped her think. But there was one thing she wanted that she did not have: an adventure. Real adventures, she was fairly sure, did not happen inside the palace. They happened in the Enchanted Forest that she could see from her window every morning, green and mysterious, with sunlight moving through it in a way that seemed almost alive. Every morning she looked at it. Every morning she thought: today. And on one particular morning, she meant it.

The Enchanted Forest was everything she had hoped it would be. The trees were older than the palace — older, perhaps, than the kingdom — and their roots rose from the ground in great curved arches that made natural seats and bridges. Flowers grew that she had no names for, in colours that didn't quite match anything she had seen before. Small creatures watched her from shadows with bright, curious eyes. And the further she walked, the quieter the world outside became, until there was nothing but the sound of leaves and her own footsteps and the occasional soft call of some bird she couldn't see. She was not frightened. She was the opposite of frightened. She was completely, wholly alive.

At the centre of the forest, where the oldest trees grew in a circle around a clearing full of soft grass, Nadia found something extraordinary: a door. Not attached to a building — simply standing on its own, covered in climbing roses, perfectly upright. She walked around it. From the back it was just a door. From the front, when she looked through the keyhole, she saw somewhere else entirely — a garden even more beautiful than the forest, full of golden light that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The door was locked. But lying in the roots of the nearest tree was a small silver key. Nadia picked it up and held it in her palm for a moment, looking at the door. Then she smiled, straightened her crown, and opened it. Some adventures, she had discovered, were waiting for you all along. THE END
The trees were her friends. They whispered secrets of the kingdom.
The animals trusted her. She helped lost fawns find their mothers.
One day, a drought threatened the kingdom. The crops were dying!
Ivy asked the forest for help. The trees knew where hidden springs were!
She led her people to fresh water! The kingdom was saved!
The King understood now. "The forest is your gift, Ivy."

Princess Ivy became the Forest Guardian - the kingdom's greatest treasure.

The End

pages.text_content: The door was no bigger than Rowan's hand — made of bark and wound through with living vines, fitting so perfectly into the hollow that you'd miss it unless you were looking. A voice came from behind it: small and old and cautious, saying words she couldn't quite make out. Rowan crouched down and put her ear close. 'Only someone truly brave and truly kind can open this door,' the voice said. Rowan thought for a long moment. She had faced plenty of challenges that required bravery. The kindness part, she thought, was actually more important. She knocked very gently. 'Please may I come in? I would love to meet you.'

The door swung inward with a sound like a sigh. Inside, in a space that seemed larger than the hollow should allow, stood a whole village of woodland sprites — no taller than Rowan's thumb, with wings like dried leaves and eyes like polished acorns. There were hundreds of them. They had been trapped inside the tree for a hundred years by an enchantment that had simply been forgotten — not cast by an enemy, just the remnant of old protective magic that had outlasted its purpose and didn't know how to end. They stared at Rowan. She stared back. Then the eldest sprite, who had a white beard down to his knees, said: 'We hoped someone would come.'

Rowan helped them out one by one, which took a considerable time because there were a great many of them and they were all quite stiff from a hundred years of standing around inside a tree. She sat on the root with her legs crossed and held each one in her cupped palms and carried them to the edge of the hollow where they could stretch their wings in the proper air. The sprites shook their wings, blinked in the dappled forest light, and made small sounds of pure relief. The silver fox sat nearby and watched the whole operation with dignified approval.

Once all the sprites were free, something extraordinary happened to the forest. It was as if it exhaled — a long slow breath through every leaf and root and branch. The mist that had hung over it for as long as anyone could remember thinned and dispersed. Sunlight came through in proper shafts, golden and warm. The trees seemed to stand differently, somehow — less hunched, more open. The eldest sprite told Rowan that the enchantment had been making the whole forest sad for a hundred years. 'We didn't know,' Rowan said. 'How could you?' said the sprite. 'You hadn't come yet.'

The sprites showed Rowan the hidden parts of the Enchanted Forest in return — the places that no human had seen in a century. A glade where every tree grew in a perfect spiral. A stream whose water was so clear it looked like glass, with fish that seemed to be made of light. A hill where the grass grew in a dozen shades of green, each shade corresponding to a different kind of luck. The eldest sprite told her the names of each thing in the old forest language, which sounded like wind in branches, and Rowan tried to remember all of it.

All too soon, the light through the trees told her it was approaching lunch and she had made a promise. The sprites gathered to see her off. The eldest handed her a tiny acorn carved with a pattern she couldn't quite read. 'Come back,' he said. 'The forest will know you now.' Rowan closed her fingers around the acorn and looked back at the village of sprites settling happily into the spaces between the roots, rediscovering their home after a century. The silver fox appeared at her side and led her back to the path. She followed it out of the trees into the ordinary morning light.

She arrived back at the palace exactly at lunch. Her boots were very muddy. Her hair was considerably more tangled than it had been. In her pocket was an acorn with a carved pattern and in her head was a forest language that sounded like wind. Her mother looked at her muddy state and sighed. Her father looked at her expression — that particular brightness in her eyes that meant something significant had happened — and said nothing, only smiled. Rowan sat down to lunch and thought about what she had learned: that sometimes the greatest magic is not what you find, but the act of knocking, gently and kindly, and asking to come in. THE END

books.title: The Dinosaur Time Machine
books.description: Two siblings accidentally travel back to the age of dinosaurs.
books.back_cover_text: When Sam and Emma fix grandpa's old machine, they didn't expect to meet real dinosaurs!

pages.text: The time machine was sitting in the school science cupboard between a broken microscope and a box of batteries, and it had a Post-it note on it that said DO NOT TOUCH in large red letters, which was unfortunately exactly the kind of note most likely to make eleven-year-old Theo touch it. He had been looking for graph paper. He found instead a device the size of a large lunchbox, with two dials, a small screen, and a green button that was practically daring him to press it. He checked that nobody was watching. The cupboard was empty. He pressed the green button. The world went sideways, then inside-out, then right again, and when Theo opened his eyes he was no longer in the science cupboard.

He was outdoors. The air was warm and heavy and smelled of plants and rain and something earthier and older than anything he had encountered before. The trees were not right — they were too large and the wrong shapes, with leaves that were enormous and ferns that came up to his shoulders. The sky was pale and wide. And from somewhere not very far away — close enough that the ground trembled very slightly with each one — came a sound. Footsteps. Very large footsteps. Theo looked down at the time machine, which had a small screen showing the number -66,000,000. He looked at the ferns. He looked at the direction the footsteps were coming from. He made several calculations very quickly. Then he climbed the nearest tree, which he felt was the only reasonable response to the situation.

The dinosaur that came through the ferns was not a terrifying one, as it turned out — it was a young Triceratops, about the size of a large car, with three magnificent horns and a frill that caught the light as it moved. It stopped below Theo's tree and looked up at him with one large, calm eye. Theo had studied dinosaurs since he was five. He knew that Triceratops were herbivores. He knew they were probably not dangerous if you didn't threaten them. He also knew that knowing these things intellectually was quite different from sitting in a tree while one looked at you. They regarded each other for a long time. Then the Triceratops made a low sound, turned, and walked away with the unhurried dignity of something that had never been in a hurry in its life. Theo climbed down. He pressed the green button. The world went sideways again, and he arrived back in the science cupboard, where the graph paper was exactly where he'd looked before. He put the Post-it note back very carefully, and went to his lesson, and said nothing to anyone. Though for the rest of the day he kept thinking about that eye. THE END
Danny landed in a prehistoric jungle. Real dinosaurs everywhere!
A friendly Triceratops let him ride! "This is AMAZING!"
He watched Pterodactyls fly and Brachiosaurus eat from tall trees.
But then - THUMP THUMP - a T-Rex appeared!
Danny remembered: T-Rex has bad eyesight! He stood very still.
The T-Rex walked away! Danny's knowledge saved him!

Back home, Danny knew: learning isn't just fun - it's powerful!

The End

pages.text_content: He spent the morning observing from a respectful distance, notebook in hand, writing everything down with shaking hands that eventually steadied. The Triceratops was part of a herd — eight adults and three juveniles who moved together through the forest, communicating in low rumbles and occasional horn gestures that Max was fairly sure had meaning. The juveniles, he noticed, played. They shoved each other with their small horns and chased each other between the adults' legs. One of them kept wandering slightly too far and being herded back by a patient adult. Dinosaur parenting, Max thought, looked familiar.

In the afternoon, he heard a different kind of sound — higher, shrieking, coming from somewhere through the trees. He moved carefully toward it and found a dry riverbed where a pair of Velociraptors were hunting. Everything the books had described was right: they were fast, they communicated with each other constantly, and they were terrifyingly intelligent. He watched one problem-solve its way around an obstacle with a patience and ingenuity that made his skin prickle. They were nothing like the movie versions. They were considerably more alarming. He stayed very still for a very long time.

The baby Stegosaurus found him. He still didn't know how — he had been sitting quietly behind a tree — but suddenly it was there, sniffing his shoe with a thoughtful expression. It was about the size of a large dog, with plates along its back that were soft and slightly translucent, not yet fully grown. Its tail swayed slowly. It investigated his notebook. It investigated his other shoe. Then it sat down heavily on his foot, which he chose to interpret as affection. He named it Socrates, which he felt was a dignified name for a dignified creature.

Socrates followed him for the rest of the day, which complicated his observations somewhat but made the day considerably better. Together they watched a herd of Ankylosaurus cross a river, slow and armoured and unstoppable.
