They witnessed a flock of Pterosaurs wheeling overhead in the orange late-afternoon sky, their calls carrying across the forest in long echoing notes. Once, in the distance, Max glimpsed something enormous moving through the trees — too large to be any of the species he'd seen so far, its footsteps shaking the ground even from half a kilometre away. He wrote T-REX? in his notebook with three question marks.

As the sun began to lower and the shadows grew long across the fern floor, Max knew he would have to go back. The machine had given him a twelve-hour window — he'd read this on a small screen inside that he hadn't noticed at first. He looked at his notes: forty-seven pages, front and back, written in his smallest handwriting. He had seen things no human being alive had ever seen. He had sat next to a Stegosaurus. He had watched Velociraptors hunt. He had breathed the air of a world sixty-six million years in the past. His hands were still shaking slightly.

He said goodbye to Socrates, which felt important even if Socrates didn't understand what goodbye meant. He patted the small dinosaur very gently on the warm side. Socrates swung its tail once, slowly, and turned back to the ferns. Max walked back to where he had landed, oriented himself carefully with his notebook, and placed his hand on the machine's return button. He looked back one last time at the prehistoric forest — the colours, the scale, the impossible aliveness of it all — and pressed the button.

The garage reformed around him. His grandfather's toolboxes. The smell of oil and dust. Outside, through the small window, the ordinary sky of an ordinary Tuesday. Max sat down on the garage floor because his legs had decided they were done. He opened his notebook to the first page and looked at his first entry: 9:14am. Arrived. There is a Triceratops. He smiled so hard his face hurt. That evening he sat at his desk and began transferring his notes into his proper field journal, every detail, every observation, every moment. He had been the only human being to ever do this. He was going to do it justice. THE END

books.title: Ocean Wonders
books.description: Explore the magical world beneath the waves.
books.back_cover_text: Dive deep into the ocean and discover amazing creatures you never knew existed!

pages.text: Beneath the waves, in the deepest, most beautiful part of the ocean, there lived a little fish named Finn. Finn was bright blue with one yellow stripe along his side, and he was absolutely certain that the small coral reef where he lived was the most wonderful place in the entire world. He knew every rock and every anemone and every crack where the shy seahorses hid. He knew where the light came through the water in long golden shafts at midday, and where the current made the sea grass dance like ribbons. But one morning, Finn's grandmother said something that changed everything. 'Have you ever swum to the Drop Off, Finn? Where the reef ends and the deep water begins?' Finn looked toward the blue darkness at the edge of his world. He never had.

The journey to the Drop Off took Finn past parts of the reef he had never visited. He swam through an archway of pink coral where tiny purple fish darted in formation like living confetti. He passed a garden of sea anemones in every colour, their tentacles swaying in a current that smelled of open water. He watched a sea turtle glide past above him with the slow, magnificent authority of something that had been swimming since before his grandparents were born. The ocean, Finn began to realise, was much larger than his small corner of it. This thought was both frightening and wonderful at the same time, which he was learning was how the best discoveries usually felt.

At the Drop Off, the reef ended and the water changed. Below him was a blue so deep it looked almost black, and it went down further than he could see. Finn hovered at the edge and looked out into it. And then — slowly, in ones and twos and then in dozens — lights appeared in the deep. Soft bioluminescent glows, drifting and pulsing in the dark water. Creatures he had no names for, lit from within, moving through the deep ocean with a graceful slowness that was completely different from anything in the reef above. Finn watched for a long time without moving. He had not known the world was this large and this beautiful. When he finally swam home and told his grandmother what he had seen, she smiled. 'The ocean never runs out of wonders,' she said. 'That is why we must never stop exploring it.' THE END
Clownfish hide in anemones. They're best friends who protect each other!
Sea turtles are ancient travelers. They swim thousands of miles!
Dolphins are the ocean's playful puppies. They talk with clicks!
Even the scary-looking sharks keep the ocean healthy!
The deep sea has creatures that GLOW! Like underwater stars!
"The ocean needs our help," Coral said. "Keep it clean and wonderful!"

Now you know ocean secrets! Go share them with the world!

The End

pages.text_content: Her dad knew a lot about the sea. He had grown up near the coast and spent his whole childhood in it. He showed Mara how to identify the different types of seaweed — the flat green sheets, the long brown ribbons, the tiny bubbled strings that popped satisfyingly when you squeezed them. He showed her how the tide had left a line of treasures along the beach: shells, pebbles worn smooth by years of tumbling in the waves, a single perfect sea glass, frosted green, with all its sharp edges softened away. He let her keep the sea glass.

In the afternoon they hired a small rowing boat and went out past the breakers into calmer water. Here the sea was a different colour — deeper, darker, a true blue-green over the sandy bottom. Mara leaned over the side and looked down. She could see for what felt like miles: sunlight making shifting patterns on the sand, a shoal of small silver fish moving as a single shimmering shape, a long ribbon of dark seagrass swaying in a current she couldn't feel from the surface. The sea had a whole sky of its own, going down instead of up.

Just before they turned back, a seal appeared. It surfaced ten metres from the boat, regarded them with large liquid eyes, then dove again in one smooth arc. Mara gripped the side of the boat. 'Will it come back?' she whispered. 'Maybe,' said her dad. They waited. Two minutes later it surfaced on the other side — closer this time, curious. Mara and the seal looked at each other for a long still moment. Then it dove again and was gone. Mara breathed out slowly. She felt as though something important had just happened, though she couldn't have said what.

That evening they ate fish and chips on the harbour wall, watching the fishing boats come in. The chips were hot and salty and the portions were enormous. Mara ate everything. The sky turned pink and orange over the water. The boats rocked gently against their ropes, their hulls knocking against the wooden pier in a slow rhythm like a heartbeat. Mara listened. The harbour, she thought, had a sound like breathing — the water going in and out, in and out, the same rhythm it had kept for thousands of years while different people sat on different harbour walls and ate their chips and watched.

Before bed, Mara sat on the floor of the cottage with her bucket of collected shells and sorted them. She had twelve different kinds — she counted carefully and looked them up in the guide from the gift shop. Scallops with their fan shape. Whelks in their spiral. Mussels with their dark blue sheen. One perfect razor clam. One she couldn't identify at all, which her dad said was the best kind. She arranged them on the windowsill in a row where the morning light would hit them, and went to sleep listening to the sound of the sea.

On the last morning, Mara got up before everyone else and walked down to the beach alone. The tide was out further than she had seen it, revealing a wide stretch of wet sand that the sea had left behind, full of its own patterns — ripples and pools and the trails of things that had moved across it in the night. The sky was pale and the sea was quiet and she had the whole beach entirely to herself. She walked to the water's edge and stood there, looking at the horizon, saying goodbye in the way you say goodbye to something enormous — not out loud, just inwardly, with your whole chest.

In the car on the way home, Mara held the green sea glass in her fist and looked out at the fields rolling past and thought about everything she had seen. The seal's eyes. The starfish. The world under the rowing boat. The way a wave felt when it lifted you. She would come back, she promised herself. She would come back every year until she knew every shell and every tide pattern and where the seals liked to surface and which rock pool held the most interesting things. There was simply far too much wonder to see it all in one visit. THE END

books.title: The Superhero School
books.description: A regular kid discovers they have superpowers on their first day at a new school.
books.back_cover_text: Jake thought he was ordinary until his first day at Hero Academy revealed his true powers!

pages.text: The letter arrived on a Tuesday morning and said, in plain black type on official cream paper: YOU HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED TO CAPE ACADEMY. Please report on Monday. Bring sensible shoes. Priya read it four times. She had not applied to Cape Academy. She had not known Cape Academy existed. She turned the letter over. On the back, in smaller print: All students are selected. None apply. You have demonstrated an ability that requires training. We look forward to meeting you. Priya thought about this carefully. She thought about the three separate occasions in the past month when she had known something was about to happen before it happened. She folded the letter and put it in her school bag. She wore her sensible shoes on Monday.

Cape Academy was inside what looked from outside like an ordinary office building on an ordinary street, but inside it opened up into something much larger than the exterior suggested — a discovery that the teacher at the front desk confirmed happened to everyone on their first day. There were thirty-two students in Priya's intake. A girl who could communicate with animals. A boy who could see the structural weakness in any physical object. Twins who shared the same dreams. None of them had known about the others. None of them had fully understood, until now, why they were different. The teacher — a small, calm woman who had apparently once stopped a bridge from collapsing using only her ability to slow down time by exactly three seconds — said the same thing to all of them: 'A power without understanding is an accident. We are here to make it something else.'

Priya's ability, they told her, was precognition — specifically, she saw events approximately ninety seconds before they happened. Not always. Not reliably. Not yet. The training was mostly about the not yet part. She spent weeks learning to stay calm when the images came, to observe them clearly rather than reacting to them immediately, to understand the difference between what was certain and what was probable. It was difficult. It was sometimes frightening. And then, on a grey Wednesday afternoon six weeks in, she saw something in her mind — a child stepping into the road, a car coming fast — and she acted on it calmly and correctly and everything was fine, and nobody who didn't know about her ability understood what she had done. This, her teacher told her afterwards, was exactly the point. 'Heroism,' she said, 'is not about being seen. It's about what happens.' Priya thought about that all the way home. Then she took out her notebook and wrote it down. THE END
"What's YOUR power?" they asked. Zoe didn't know yet. "I'm still figuring it out..."
In Power Class, nothing happened. No flying. No lasers. Nothing.
But during lunch, a bully was being mean to a small kid. Zoe stepped in.
"That's not cool," she said bravely. Everyone stopped. The bully walked away.
"Zoe! You have the power of COURAGE!" said the headmaster. "The rarest power of all!"
Zoe learned that being brave doesn't mean you're not scared—it means you do the right thing anyway.

She became the hero everyone looked up to—not for what she could do, but for who she was.

The End

pages.text_content: Nadia's cape shimmered at the edge of grey, the faintest silver beginning to show. Ms Marvel noticed but said nothing yet. In the classroom debrief, she asked each student what power they had used on the kitten problem. 'Strength,' said Theo. 'Speed,' said Suki. 'Analysis,' said Reed. Then she looked at Nadia. 'I just thought about what the kitten actually needed,' Nadia said. 'Rather than what I could do.' Ms Marvel wrote something on the board: PROBLEM DEFINITION. 'The most powerful skill in heroism,' she said, 'is understanding what problem you're actually solving before you try to solve it.'

Hero History classes were Nadia's favourite. They studied heroes throughout time — not the ones with the most impressive powers, but the ones who had made the most difference. She was particularly interested in those who had solved problems that everyone else was solving wrong. A water engineer who ended a drought not by making it rain but by redesigning how water was stored. A negotiator who ended a conflict not by overpowering either side but by finding the one thing they both actually needed. 'These people had grey capes,' Nadia said to Ms Marvel after class. 'Almost certainly,' Ms Marvel agreed.

The academy's annual Challenges week came in October. Each student faced a series of problems designed to test their specific powers. The others had straightforward tests: lift this, run here, answer this. Nadia's tests were different. She was given situations — a team that wasn't working, a resource that wasn't being used well, a conflict that had no obvious solution — and asked to improve them. She approached each one the same way: first understand exactly what the problem was, then find the simplest intervention that changed it. She solved every one. Her cape turned noticeably silver by the end of day three.

Theo asked her to help him with something. He was enormously strong but kept accidentally breaking things — doors, chairs, equipment — because he didn't know his own power yet. 'What am I doing wrong?' he asked. Nadia watched him try to open a door and immediately saw it: he was applying strength uniformly instead of calibrating it. 'You're solving every problem at maximum,' she said. 'Try ten percent first and scale up.' Theo tried it. The door opened intact. He stared at his hands. 'How did you see that?' he asked. Nadia shrugged. 'I watched what you were actually doing.' It was the most useful thing anyone had said to him since he'd arrived.

Word spread through Heroic Heights that Nadia could help you understand your own power better than you could yourself. Students started finding her at lunch, at break, in the corridors between classes. She never told anyone what to do — she just asked questions, the right questions, until they saw it themselves. Ms Marvel watched this from a distance with quiet satisfaction. She had taught at Heroic Heights for twenty years and had seen many impressive powers. She had rarely seen one this rare. She updated Nadia's file with a single new entry under power classification: Insight.

Near the end of term, Heroic Heights faced a real problem. A section of the school's foundations had developed a crack that the structural engineer said was serious. The students were given the challenge for real: solve this problem before the affected wing had to close. Teams formed — strength teams to shore up walls, speed teams to evacuate equipment, intelligence teams to model solutions. Nadia was given team leadership, which surprised her. She sat everyone down and spent twenty minutes just asking questions before she let anyone do anything. When they finally acted, they acted correctly, and the problem took four hours instead of the estimated two days.

On the last day of term, capes were reassessed. One by one, students went to the front and their capes shimmered into whatever they had become. Theo's deepened red. Suki's blazed blue. Reed's shone gold. When Nadia stood at the front, her cape blazed so brilliantly silver that students shielded their eyes. It was not a colour she had seen on any cape before. 'Silver and grey,' said Ms Marvel quietly, 'make platinum.' She held up the assembly register. On the first page, in the column for most valuable students: Nadia's name, at the top, with a star. Not because she was the strongest or the fastest or the cleverest. Because she helped everyone else be better. THE END

books.title: Cooking Adventures with Chef Cat
books.description: Chef Cat teaches kids fun and easy recipes.
books.back_cover_text: Learn to make delicious treats with Chef Cat's simple recipes that kids can make!

pages.text: In the cosiest kitchen in the whole neighbourhood, there lived a cat named Chef Cat. She wore a tall white hat that was slightly too big and always slid down over one ear, and a striped apron with pockets full of wooden spoons. Every morning she woke up early, stretched her paws, and thought about what wonderful thing she would cook today. Cooking, she believed with her whole heart, was the best magic in the world — because you could share it with everyone you loved.

Today, Chef Cat had decided to bake a birthday cake for her friend Rabbit. Rabbit's favourite colour was orange, so Chef Cat thought: carrot cake! She climbed onto her little step stool and began pulling ingredients from the shelves. Flour, sugar, butter, eggs, and three of the finest carrots from her garden, which she had grown herself in a pot by the sunny window. She lined them all up on the counter and looked at them with great satisfaction. 'Perfect,' she said to nobody in particular, because saying things out loud made them feel more official.

The mixing was Chef Cat's favourite part. She tipped the flour into the big blue bowl with a satisfying cloud of white, cracked the eggs with a decisive tap, and grated the carrots until her paws were faintly orange. She stirred everything together in big, happy circles, humming to herself as she worked. Baking smelled like warmth. It smelled like someone thinking about you. She poured the mixture into a round tin and slid it carefully into the oven, then sat on her step stool to wait, which was the hardest part.

While the cake was baking, Chef Cat made the icing — cream cheese and orange zest and a spoonful of honey, whipped together until it was smooth and fluffy and smelled extraordinary. She tasted it with a clean spoon and her eyes went very wide. She tasted it again just to be sure. Then she put the bowl in the fridge before she could eat any more of it, which she felt showed admirable self-control. The kitchen was warm and smelled of carrots and spice and something sweet, and outside the window the first snow of winter was just beginning to fall.

When Rabbit arrived that afternoon and saw the cake — three layers, orange icing, decorated with tiny marzipan carrots that Chef Cat had spent a happy hour making — she put both paws over her mouth and her eyes went very bright. 'You made this for me?' she said. 'Of course,' said Chef Cat. 'Sit down. I will cut you the biggest piece.' They sat together at the kitchen table as the snow fell outside, and Rabbit said it was the best cake she had ever tasted, and Chef Cat said that was because it had been made with the best ingredient of all. 'What is that?' asked Rabbit. Chef Cat smiled and passed her another slice. 'Knowing exactly who it is for,' she said. THE END
"Whole grains keep us running!" They baked yummy wheat muffins.
"Milk makes bones strong!" Whiskers made a banana smoothie. DELICIOUS!
"The secret ingredient is always LOVE," Chef Whiskers purred.
They had a feast! Everything was healthy AND tasty!

"Now YOU can be a chef! Cook with love and eat your colors!"

The End

pages.text_content: Then disaster struck. Bear stirred so enthusiastically that a great wave of soup splashed right over the edge of the pot and onto the kitchen floor. Mouse squeaked and jumped back. Rabbit gasped. Bear's ears drooped all the way down and he looked ready to cry. 'I've ruined it,' he said in a very small voice for such a very large bear. But Chef Cat simply laughed, reached calmly for a cloth, and began mopping up. 'Every cook in the world has spilled something,' she said cheerfully. 'The secret is to simply keep going.'

They cleaned up together — Rabbit mopping, Mouse wringing out the cloth with her tiny paws, Bear carefully checking the pot still had enough soup inside. It did. They tasted it cautiously from small spoons. The soup was warm and sweet and the ginger gave it a lovely gentle heat. 'It's wonderful,' said Rabbit, eyes wide. 'It tastes like autumn,' said Mouse, writing this down carefully in her notebook. Bear had three spoonfuls without saying anything at all, which everyone agreed was the best possible review.

Chef Cat showed them what to do next. The soup needed to be blended until it was perfectly smooth and velvety. She passed the blending stick carefully to each of them in turn. Rabbit blended too fast and made it splatter. Mouse blended very carefully and did it perfectly. Bear blended with one paw while eating a carrot he'd found on the counter with the other. 'Focus, Bear,' said Chef Cat. Bear put the carrot down with great dignity. The soup became smooth and golden and absolutely beautiful.

Now came the toppings — Chef Cat's favourite part. She set out little bowls of things: a swirl of cream, chopped fresh herbs that smelled of the garden, a sprinkle of toasted seeds that crackled satisfyingly between the teeth. Each of them decorated their own bowl. Mouse made a very precise pattern with the herbs. Rabbit added extra cream. Bear put a bit of everything on, some of it in the soup and some of it beside the soup, and pronounced this 'experimental presentation.' Chef Cat said it was very advanced.

They sat around the kitchen table together, four friends and four bowls of soup they had made with their own hands and paws. The kitchen was warm and smelled of ginger and herbs and happiness. Outside, the autumn wind blew leaves past the window. Inside, spoons clinked against bowls. Nobody spoke for a little while because they were too busy eating. 'I didn't know I could make something this good,' Rabbit said eventually. 'I didn't know cooking felt like this,' said Mouse softly, closing her notebook because some moments don't need to be written down.

After the washing up — which Bear did, insisting, though the bowls looked rather small in his great paws — they sat together with cups of warm tea. Chef Cat pulled out her recipe book and showed them the next recipe she planned to teach: a layered vegetable pie with a golden pastry top. Rabbit's eyes went wide. Mouse immediately reopened her notebook. Bear leaned forward with an expression of absolute serious dedication. 'Same time next week?' said Chef Cat. Three voices answered at once: 'Yes please.'

Walking home through the autumn leaves, each of them carried something. Rabbit carried the leftover soup in a jar for her supper. Mouse carried her recipe notebook, now with four new pages filled. Bear carried the wooden spoon, which Chef Cat had given him as a gift because he had stirred with such commitment. And all three of them carried something that couldn't be put in a jar or a notebook or held in a paw — the warm knowledge that they had made something wonderful together, and that next week, they would make something wonderful again. THE END

books.title: The Haunted Treehouse
books.description: Three friends investigate strange sounds coming from an old treehouse.
books.back_cover_text: Is the old treehouse really haunted? Join the Mystery Kids as they find out the truth!

pages.text: Everyone in Maple Street knew the treehouse was haunted. It sat at the top of the old oak at the end of number forty-two's garden, and the family who owned the house had moved away three years ago and left it behind. The rope ladder creaked in no wind. Sometimes lights appeared in the small window at night. Maisie had heard all the stories, catalogued them carefully in a notebook, and concluded that they were probably not true — but that finding out for certain would be a much better way to spend a Saturday than anything else available.

She climbed the rope ladder on a grey October afternoon with her notebook, a torch, and a flask of hot chocolate that her mother had pressed on her without asking why she needed it. The treehouse was one room, about the size of a large wardrobe, smelling of old wood and pine sap. Someone had left a blanket. Someone had left a jar of pebbles, carefully arranged by size. And on the wall, in neat handwriting that had faded to grey, was a list: THINGS I SAW FROM HERE: a fox with three cubs, the Hendersons' cat on the roof, a shooting star (Tuesday, August). Maisie sat down on the blanket and read the list three times.

The lights, it turned out, were fireflies. A whole colony of them lived in the hollow of a branch just below the treehouse floor, and on mild evenings they drifted up through a gap in the boards and floated around the small room in their dozens, which explained everything and was, Maisie felt, actually better than a ghost. She added a page to her notebook: CASE CLOSED — NOT HAUNTED. Then, because she liked it, she added: THOUGH POSSIBLY ENCHANTED, which seemed more accurate. She started her own list on the wall. The first entry read: October 14th — fireflies, dozens of them, green-gold. Maisie, age 11. She left the blanket. She left the pebbles. She came back the following Saturday, and the one after that. THE END
Creak! The floor groaned. "Who's there?" Emma called.
Something moved in the corner! Emma pointed her light...
It was a family of raccoons! They had made the treehouse their home!
The "spooky sounds" were just babies playing at night!
"You can stay," Emma smiled. She built them a special corner.
Now Emma and the raccoons share the treehouse! Best roommates ever!

The "haunted" treehouse became the coolest clubhouse in town!

The End

pages.text_content: Pip told her. He had been ten years old in 1974 when the treehouse was built by a boy named Thomas who had been his best friend. They had spent three summers up here, reading comics and using the telescope and making plans for adventures they were going to have. Then Thomas's family had moved away and Pip had gone home one afternoon and his family had moved away too, and somehow — this was the part he found hardest to explain — Pip had come back to the treehouse instead of following them. He had been here ever since. 'Waiting for Thomas?' Priya asked. Pip was quiet for a moment. 'Waiting for someone,' he said.

Priya looked at the comic books. The top one had a date on it: July 1977. She looked at the telescope, pointed at its gap in the boards. She looked at Pip, floating quietly in his corner, glowing with the soft patience of someone who has been in one place for a very long time. 'I could fix the telescope,' she said. Pip's glow flickered, which she was learning to read as surprise. 'You can't fix it. It's broken.' 'I know how to fix telescopes,' said Priya, which was true — her dad had one and had taught her the mechanics of them when she was seven. 'Oh,' said Pip. Another flicker. 'All right then.'

She brought tools the next afternoon. The telescope needed a new lens mount, which she fashioned from a piece of metal pipe she found in her dad's garage, and a cleaning and realignment of the mirrors inside. Pip watched with intense interest, occasionally floating closer to look at what she was doing and occasionally drifting away again when he felt he was in the way. By the time she was done, the telescope pointed through the gap in the boards at a patch of evening sky in which two stars were already visible. Pip pressed his face — or the approximation of a face that he had — to the eyepiece. He went very still. 'I forgot,' he said softly. 'I forgot how many there were.'

She brought the comic books back the next week — found the same series at a second-hand book fair, the issues Pip didn't have from the years after Thomas left. She read them aloud because Pip's hands couldn't turn pages. He listened with the complete absorption of someone who had been waiting a very long time for a story to continue. Occasionally he would make a small sound of satisfaction when something he had been hoping would happen happened. Occasionally he would make a sound of outrage when it didn't. 'You're very emotionally invested for a ghost,' Priya told him. 'I've had a lot of time to develop feelings about comics,' Pip said with dignity.

Word got out, because word always gets out. By the third week, Priya's friend Josie had climbed up to see for herself. Then Josie's brother. Then three other children from the road, who had been daring each other to approach the treehouse for years and now could do it because someone else had gone first. Pip was initially apprehensive. He had been a source of fear for so long that being a source of interest felt strange. But these children were curious and kind and they brought snacks and new comics and treated the treehouse with the respect it deserved, and Pip found, to his considerable surprise, that he liked them.

They fixed the treehouse up together over several weekends. New boards where the old ones had rotted. A proper curtain for the window gap. A shelf for the comic collection. The rope ladder was replaced with a proper wooden ladder that Josie's dad helped build. Pip couldn't help with any of it physically, but he directed operations with enthusiasm and a photographic memory of where everything had originally been. 'The telescope goes on the left,' he would say. 'Thomas always kept it on the left.' They put it on the left. Some things, Priya understood, were worth doing exactly right.

One evening in autumn, Priya climbed up to find Pip looking different — steadier, somehow. Less apologetically uncertain. More simply present. The treehouse was warm with the smell of old wood and the new curtain moved in a breeze through the repaired window. The comic collection was complete on its shelf. The telescope pointed at the stars. 'You're not really haunting it anymore, are you,' Priya said. It wasn't quite a question. Pip considered this. 'No,' he said. 'I think I'm just living here now.' Priya smiled. The treehouse had never, she thought, been haunted at all. It had just been waiting for the right people to fill it up again. THE END

books.title: Galaxy Racers
books.description: Kids from different planets compete in the ultimate space race.
books.back_cover_text: In the year 3000, the biggest race in the galaxy is about to begin. Who will win?

pages.text: The most important race in the galaxy happened once every ten years, and this year, for the first time in the history of the Junior Division, the favourite to win was a twelve-year-old girl from a small moon nobody had heard of. Her name was Mira, her ship was called the Sandpiper, and she had spent the last three years building it herself in her family's garage from salvaged parts and stubbornness. The Sandpiper was not beautiful in any conventional sense — it was asymmetric in a way that made engineers wince, and it had been painted three different colours at three different stages of construction and nobody had bothered to make it consistent. But Mira knew exactly what it could do, because she had made it do things that the engineers at the big racing academies said weren't possible.

The night before the race, Mira sat in the Sandpiper's cockpit with all the systems off and the canopy open and looked at the stars. The racing academy pilots — the ones with sponsor logos on their uniforms and ships that cost more than her entire moon's annual budget — were in the preparation facility being coached by teams of specialists. Mira had her notes, a sandwich her father had made her, and a very clear picture in her head of every turn on the course. She had memorised it not just as data but as feeling — the way each bend would pull at her stomach, the places where the gravitational currents changed. She finished the sandwich, closed the canopy, and went to sleep in her pilot's seat. She had done everything she could. Tomorrow she would fly.

At the halfway point of the race, Mira was in third place and gaining. The Sandpiper moved through the asteroid field with a precision that made the commentary team go quiet for a moment — not because it was showy, but because it was so exactly right, every tiny adjustment so perfectly timed, that it looked effortless in a way that only truly practised things look effortless. The pilot in second place was good. The one in first was excellent. But Mira had something they didn't have: she had built her ship, which meant she knew it the way you know something you've made yourself — not just its capabilities but its character, its particular strengths, the way it responded to her instinctively. She found her line through a gap that no other pilot had attempted and she flew it clean. When she crossed the finish line first, she did not shout or pump her fist. She just breathed out, very slowly, and patted the dashboard gently. 'Good girl,' she told the Sandpiper. 'I knew you could.' THE END
Race day! Ships from every planet lined up. Star was nervous.
The race went through asteroid belts, around moons, and through star gates!
Star was behind! But she knew a shortcut through the Nebula Cloud!
The clouds were thick, but Star trusted her instincts.
She shot out of the nebula - in FIRST PLACE!
Crossing the finish line, the crowd went wild! Star had WON!

"Dream big, fly fast, never give up!" Star told young fans.

The End

pages.text_content: Blaze immediately shot to the front, his enormous engines leaving a blazing red trail across the stars. Rex was right behind him, boosters screaming. The twins threaded through traffic with practised elegance. Zara let them all go. She had studied the course for two years and she knew something they didn't: the first asteroid field had a narrow corridor on the lower route that nobody ever took because it looked too tight. It wasn't. She dropped her nose and cut through it at full speed, saving forty-seven seconds.

By the time they reached the nebula section, Zara had moved up to eighth place just by flying smart. The nebula was the most beautiful part of the race — clouds of gas in pink and gold and violet, so thick you navigated by instruments alone. Zara had memorised the instrument readings she needed. Some pilots slowed down in the nebula, frightened by the reduced visibility. Zara did not slow down. She came out of the nebula in fourth place and heard a surprised cheer crackle through her radio from someone watching at home.

Saturn's rings were next — the most dangerous section. The rings were made of ice and rock, some pieces the size of a fist and some the size of a house, and they moved constantly. You could not plan your route through the rings. You had to read them as you went, making split-second decisions, trusting your instincts. This was where Zara came alive. Her hands moved across the controls with a fluency that felt like music. She wove through the rings, under a tumbling boulder, over a flat sheet of ice, tight left past a spinning cluster, and out the other side in second place.

Blaze was first, just ahead of her. He had been in first place for the whole race and his confidence showed in the way he flew — fast but relaxed, certain of his victory. He hadn't noticed Zara moving up through the field because she had done it quietly and cleverly. Now she was right behind him with one section left: the long straight home past the moons of Jupiter, where engines and fuel management determined everything. Zara checked her fuel gauge. She had saved more than anyone. She smiled.

She opened the Silver Spark's engine to full for the first time in the entire race. The little ship surged forward with a sound like thunder. Blaze heard her coming and pushed his own throttle further — but he had been running at full power all race and had less in reserve. Zara pulled alongside him. He looked across at her — this small dented silver ship, this girl nobody had heard of — and she could see even through his visor that he was surprised. She pulled ahead. One kilometre from the finish she crossed into the lead.

The Silver Spark crossed the finish line first. For a moment Zara just sat there in the sudden quiet of the cockpit, hands still on the controls, heart hammering. Then the radio exploded with voices — the race commentator, her dad, her team, the crowd. She pulled off her helmet and looked out at the stars through the porthole — the same stars she had looked at from her bedroom window and promised herself she would one day race through. She had done it. She pressed her hand against the sticker above the controls.

On the podium, they gave her the golden comet trophy. It was heavier than she expected and it caught the light beautifully. Blaze stood next to her, and after a moment he held out his hand. She shook it. 'Good race,' he said, and she could tell he meant it. Her dad found her afterwards in the crowd and hugged her so hard her feet left the ground. 'Smart flying,' he said into her hair. 'Smart flying wins races.' The Wall of Champions on the moon of Arcturus had a new name on it. It was hers. THE END
